{"category":"convention","enforced":true,"name":"Design intent moves only on the owner's word — an agent may propose anything and settle nothing","statement":"A NODE THAT ASSERTS INTENT REACHES A SETTLED STATE ONLY BECAUSE ANTHONY SAID SO. An agent may create, draft, measure, argue and recommend without limit; it may not move a Requirement off `proposed`, mark a Decision `accepted`, or record a rule's enforcement on his behalf. Alex is a genuine design contributor and second user (`who:alex`), and his input is ADVISORY — it informs and gates nothing.

ENFORCED — Anthony, 2026-08-09, answering the consequence question directly ("if a session recorded a decision as accepted without you saying so, should that stop the build, or is it advice?"): stop the build.

⭐ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, and it was not predicted. Asked the same question about the branch-then-PR process rule minutes earlier, he answered ADVICE. So in a one-developer project the PROCESS rule is self-discipline and the AUTHORITY rule is inviolable — the opposite of the naive expectation that a solo project needs no authority modelling because there is only one person. What one person needs protection from is not another person; it is an AGENT WRITING IN HIS VOICE. That is a data point for `req:a-node-can-say-who-may-change-it` from the simple end of the scale, where every other data point so far came from a multi-agent fleet.

WHAT IT OWES, stated plainly rather than quietly closed: a DETECTOR. `unverified_enforced_rule` will fire at 0.6 and stay until a PASSING Verification is attached — a `planned` one does not silence it. NO CHECK IS ATTACHED TODAY, deliberately: the governance-proposal skill's standing warning is that attaching a check to close a finding is green-washing, and a passing check that tests nothing is a lie the graph cannot see.

THE CHECK THAT WOULD ACTUALLY DETECT IT, so the debt is specific rather than vague: every Decision at `accepted` carries an AUTHORED_BY edge to `who:ajs`, and every Requirement off `proposed` likewise. This is unusually checkable for a governance rule — the graph already holds the edge, and `loop_status` already computes the mirror image (a `proposed` Decision with an approver who has not answered). What is missing is the inverse: a SETTLED node with nobody's name on it.

ALREADY PARTLY MECHANIZED, which is why enforcement is not a bluff: `add_decision` lands at `proposed`; `add_requirement` lands at `proposed`; `dec:certainty-derived` derives a requirement's certainty from status × provenance because every move off `proposed` records the user's word; `set_requirement_status`'s own guardrail says promoting it yourself forges their signature; and `dec:three-party-checks` states the division — the LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides. The rule names the policy those mechanisms serve, which until now was implemented everywhere and stated nowhere.

HONEST BOUND: the tooling resists the violation but cannot presently REPORT one, which is exactly the gap the enforcement flag now makes visible instead of leaving to good behaviour."}
